title: Iran Fires Missiles at Israel for the First Time Since April. Oil Surges Past $93.
excerpt: The attack came hours after Israel struck Beirut. Oil jumped more than three per cent. India, which imports 85 per cent of its crude, is watching the Strait of Hormuz more nervously than ever.
body:
Iran launched multiple waves of ballistic missiles at Israel on Sunday evening, the first direct Iranian attack on Israeli soil since the ceasefire took hold in early April. Israeli defence systems intercepted the incoming missiles, and there were no immediate reports of casualties. But the escalation shattered a fragile calm that had held for sixty-one days — and sent tremors through energy markets that India cannot afford to ignore.

The Israeli military confirmed three distinct waves of launches from Iranian territory. Air-raid sirens sounded across northern and central Israel. "Defensive systems are operating to intercept the threat," the IDF posted on X within minutes of the first detection.

## What Triggered the Attack

The missile salvos followed an Israeli airstrike on Beirut's Dahiyeh district earlier on Sunday — the first Israeli military action in the Lebanese capital since Washington announced a truce plan for Lebanon last week. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the strike targeted a Hezbollah command centre, in response to two projectiles that Hezbollah had fired across the northern border.

Iran's parliamentary speaker Mohammed Baqer Qalibaf, who has served as Tehran's chief negotiator, called the Beirut strike a "violation of agreements over Lebanon" and declared U.S. bases and Israeli assets legitimate targets. Hardline lawmaker Ebrahim Rezaei went further, posting on X that Iran would deliver a "decisive and painful response."

## Trump Urges Restraint — on Both Sides

President Donald Trump, briefed at his golf club in Bedminster, New Jersey, moved quickly to contain the spiral. "You've shot your missiles, that's enough," he told Fox News. "Get back to the table and make a deal." He told Axios he would call Netanyahu and press him not to retaliate.

His comments came on the same day NBC broadcast a pre-recorded interview marking 100 days of the conflict. "We're very close to a deal, or I'm going to blow the hell out of them," Trump said — a line that captured the carrot-and-stick calculus that has defined Washington's Iran policy since February.

An Israeli official responded bluntly: any attack on Israeli territory from Iran would be met with retaliation and considered "an opportunity to renew the campaign."

## Oil Prices Jump, Hormuz Uncertainty Deepens

West Texas Intermediate crude futures surged more than three per cent on Sunday night, pushing toward $94 a barrel. Brent crude, already trading around $93 after Friday's settlement, is expected to open higher when Asian markets resume trading on Monday. The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 20 per cent of the world's oil transited before the war, remains effectively closed and under Iranian control.

JPMorgan had predicted the strait would reopen this month. That forecast now looks optimistic. Each additional month of closure adds an estimated $5 a barrel to third-quarter oil price projections and $15 per barrel to the fourth quarter, as global inventories continue to shrink.

## What This Means for India

India consumes approximately 5.5 million barrels of crude oil daily and imports about 85 per cent of it. Before the war, roughly 45 per cent of India's crude imports passed through or near the Strait of Hormuz. That share has dropped to about 30 per cent as Indian refiners have scrambled to diversify, turning to Russia, Venezuela, Brazil, Angola and Nigeria.

But diversification has a price. India is paying a 425 per cent higher premium for Russian crude compared with pre-war rates. The country's import bill — already swollen by prices stabilising near $100 a barrel — faces further upward pressure if the strait stays shut.

There is also the human dimension. More than eight million Indian citizens live and work in Gulf states — Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Oman. Iran fired seven ballistic missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain on Friday alone. Kuwait's army said the missiles passed over residential areas. India evacuated approximately 52,000 nationals from the Gulf in the early weeks of the crisis, but millions remain.

Sunday's escalation makes a near-term deal between Washington and Tehran harder, not easier. Tehran's demands — lifting all sanctions, recognition of its control over the strait, and release of $24 billion in frozen assets — remain far from what Washington is willing to offer. The prospect of Iranian assets being redirected to repair damage in Gulf states, which a U.S. source confirmed on Saturday, adds another irritant to already poisoned negotiations.

For India, every week the strait remains closed is another week of higher fuel costs, tighter LPG supplies — 90 per cent of India's LPG imports transit Hormuz — and quiet anxiety about the safety of its largest overseas diaspora.

**Sources:** Reuters, Wall Street Journal, MarketWatch, Barron's, Devdiscourse, Fox News
